summary: A correction to RFC 107. At the end of its flow control section, the range for a fraction should read zero to 127 rather than zero to 128. The allocation is returned only when the leftmost bit is 1. It was replaced by RFC 154.

eli5.summary: A note fixes one number in a rulebook, saying the count should stop at 127. The first number given was one too high.

questions: what is the error in rfc 107 flow control
what is the correct range in rfc 107 flow control
subtitle: A correction to a range specification in RFC 107's flow control section.

tldr.problem: RFC 107 contains an error in its flow control section: it specifies a range from zero to 128, which is off by one.
tldr.mechanism: The correct range should be zero to 127, allowing for 128 distinct values as intended. The allocation should be returned only when the high-order (leftmost) bit of the corresponding fraction is 1.
tldr.outcome: This one-page correction clarifies the specification, but was itself superseded by RFC 154, which presumably incorporated this and other clarifications.

today: RFC 132 is historic and has been obsoleted by RFC 154. It is an example of the early RFC process, where corrections and clarifications were issued as separate notes rather than through the errata system that came later.

sections.title: The Error
sections.content: This one-page note by Jim White of UCSB points out a typographical error in RFC 107. On page 5 of that RFC, in the section titled 'V. Flow Control', there is a partial sentence that reads: 'Each of these numbers is interpreted as "the number of 128ths of the current allocation" to be returned if it is in the range zero to 128...' The range is incorrect; it should read 'if it is in the range of zero to 127...' with only 127 as the upper bound.
sections.eli5: RFC 107 says a number should be between 0 and 128, but 0 to 128 gives you 129 slots. It should say 0 to 127 to get 128 slots.

sections.title: Allocation Logic
sections.content: The correction clarifies that the allocation is to be returned only when the high-order bit of the corresponding fraction is 1. By specifying the range as zero to 127 rather than zero to 128, the protocol correctly maps an 8-bit field to 128 distinct states (0 through 127), which is the standard interpretation.
sections.eli5: When the first bit is 1, you return all your allocation. The range zero to 127 makes this work correctly with an 8-bit number.

sections.title: Why This Matters
sections.content: Off-by-one errors in protocol specifications can cause subtle but serious problems. An endpoint that implements the range zero to 128 (129 values) will behave differently than one using zero to 127 (128 values), causing interoperability failures or incorrect flow control behavior. Early RFC corrections like this one were important for maintaining consistency across the emerging ARPA network implementations.
sections.eli5: Getting the number wrong breaks the protocol. That is why even tiny corrections like this one mattered in the early internet.
